body:
Watch the BJP supporter at the CJP protest.

1. His son studied 12 hours a day for two years.
2. He and his brother-in-law took loans and mortgaged their land to fund it.
3. Then the NEET paper leaked. He says it plainly: this didn't destroy his kid's future, it destroyed their future.
4. He's a Sanghi. He'll probably still vote for Modi. But even he is now saying it out loud, "BJP leaders send their kids abroad while we suffer," and demanding Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation.

That's the whole point.

The hardcore Sanghi voter won't move. Nothing shifts them. But this man isn't the target.

The target is the huge silent crowd watching him, the fence-sitters who can be persuaded.

When they see even BJP's own people hurting, one thought lands: if the party does this to its own loyalists, what will it do to us?

And here's what people forget.

In 2024, BJP's vote share fell by just 0.77%.

That tiny drop took them from 303 seats to 240. In our electoral system, a small shift in votes becomes a huge shift in seats.

Now add the rest: no jobs, rising prices, economic misery, one leaked exam after another. Anger like that doesn't stay quiet. It spreads.

CJP's strength is that it belongs to no party. That's exactly why it works.

A disenchanted BJP voter listens to another disenchanted BJP voter, but would not talk to me, you, or even Congress. Because that's how much India has changed.

CJP can do what no party can: stoke the disappointment, start the anger.

But anger needs somewhere to go. Fire needs a path. CJP can light it, but someone still has to be the destination that turns that anger into votes.

So the job is simple. Let the CJP light the fire. And Congress should build the channel to carry it. That's how 240 becomes less than 150.

This is purely electoral math, votes and seats, not about me. Criticise me all you want; the numbers stay the same.

body:
These CJP protesters have no clue who or what they’re actually backing - and that’s exactly the point.

Take the viral clip of that protester (Ujjwal) from the Jantar Mantar event. He joins a protest demanding the Education Minister’s resignation over NEET leaks and exam scams, but when asked point-blank about Umar Khalid, he blanks out or dodges. Classic example.

Most rank-and-file “cockroaches” are just frustrated Gen-Z kids angry about real issues - paper leaks, unemployment, broken education system. Fair enough. But they’re being herded into a movement whose core leadership has a documented history of aligning with figures and narratives widely seen as anti-national.

The leadership angle:

•  Founder Abhijeet Dipke (the guy who started it all as “satire”): Former AAP social media/comms volunteer. Old posts and statements show him defending or supporting Umar Khalid (the same activist accused in the Delhi riots conspiracy case under UAPA). Critics like Arnab Goswami have grilled him directly on AAP links, “tukde-tukde” narratives, and apparent support for controversial separatist-leaning voices. The protest timing even overlapped with Umar Khalid-related developments, and some CJP events/chants reportedly shifted from “NEET accountability” to “Umar Khalid is our leader” vibes.

•  Official spokespersons:

•  Saurav Das (chief spokesperson): Investigative journalist with a track record of sharp attacks on the judiciary and cases tied to AAP figures.

•  Vijeta Dahiya: Political researcher/filmmaker/content creator closely associated with Dhruv Rathee’s circle (known for heavy anti-government content).

•  Ashutosh Ranka: IIT-LSE background, with past AAP-adjacent connections reported in some circles.

This isn’t some organic, leaderless youth uprising. It’s a movement started by someone with clear past ties to AAP (a party often accused by nationalists of soft-pedaling on national security issues) and spokespeople from the same ideological ecosystem.

The real agenda claim:

Critics say it’s not about fixing exams — it’s about manufacturing chaos and riots under the cover of “youth anger.”

•  Genuine student frustration gets hijacked.

•  Protests that start on education quickly get polluted with slogans for jailed activists like Umar Khalid.

•  The “cockroach” branding and calls for “ruckus” (in some old videos) get framed as resilience, but opponents call it deliberate destabilization — especially with the founder operating partly from the US while pushing street action in India.

body:
In the last five months, three major protests have taken place against the Education Ministry:

▪️GC protest against the UGC Act
▪️NSUI protest against the NEET paper leak
▪️Cockroach protest against the NEET paper leak

Surprisingly, despite being backed by significant financial resources (Cockroach Party) and strong organisational strength (NSUI), both CJP and NSUI failed to achieve their objectives. In contrast, the GC group, a relatively small network of online protesters, succeeded in drawing institutional attention, securing a stay order from the Supreme Court, and forcing the government to backtrack.

This outcome is precisely why OSINT researchers like me got curious to examine what enabled the GC group to succeed where the Cockroach and NSUI efforts fell short.

Key reasons behind the GC group’s success:

1. Solution-centric approach: The GC group focused on solutions. They carefully analysed the process, identified critical flaws, and targeted them directly. In contrast, CJP and NSUI did not appear serious about delivering solutions. They seemed more invested in political point-scoring, which made their approach lack sincerity and credibility.

2. Constitutional methods + powerful messaging: The GC group chose the constitutional route by filing a petition in the Supreme Court. They complemented this with clear, compelling social media messaging that cut through the noise and even drew support from pro-BJP handles.

On the other side, NSUI failed to generate any meaningful social media buzz. CJP created some noise, but it lacked focus, clarity, and impact. Their reliance on street protests without a sharp narrative ultimately limited their effectiveness.

GC group kept their movement non-political and didnt carry any political baggage while NUSI protest was completely political and CJP tried to show them non-political but exposed badly in this

The GC group’s success, set against the failures of CJP and NSUI, offers a clear case study in how to achieve tangible results in today’s environment.

Key takeaways:
1. Solution focus beats political theatre
2. Constitutional + digital hybrid outperforms street activism
3. Authentic non-partisan positioning is a force multiplier
4. Strategy and narrative discipline is more powerful than money and organisation

Paper Leaks Problem - What to do

1. Map out the full process
Break down the issue end-to-end to understand exactly how it functions.

2. Identify the bottlenecks
Pinpoint the specific flaws, gaps, or points of failure in the system.

3. Offer a robust solution
Present a clear, practical, and well-reasoned alternative instead of mere criticism.

4. Create focused social media buzz
Build strong narrative momentum around your solution with sharp, solution-oriented messaging.

5. Engage the government constructively
Treat the government as a partner, not an enemy. They too want improvement and will respond positively to sincere, well-presented solutions.

6. Approach the courts if required
If the government fails to act, escalate through constitutional means by filing a petition in the appropriate court.

body:
Left-wing students’ organisation All India Students’ Association (AISA) recently announced a week-long nationwide campaign ‘Cockroaches on the streets’, across Delhi, demanding the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. The campaign began yesterday (11th June) and will continue till 18th June. Yesterday, AISA members wearing cockroach masks protested in Delhi University’s North Campus, Kamla Nagar, Patel Chest, Gurmandi and Vijaynagar.

This comes days after the Left-wing students’ organisation joined the farcical Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) protest held at Jantar Mantar in Delhi on 6th June. The protest was organised in the name of demanding the resignation of the Union Education Minister for the recent NEET exam paper leak and raising issues related to students. However, the ground reality of the protest revealed a different story, where Leftist organisations like the AISA were seen raising slogans of ‘Azadi-Azadi’ and ‘Jai Bheem’.

While AISA has not officially declared its support for the CJP, the All India President of AISA, Neha Bora, was at the forefront of the CJP protest. It is no secret that Left-wing students organistions like the AISA push their ideological and political agenda in the guise of raising students’ issues. And that’s exactly what Bora was seen doing in the pretext of demanding reforms in the education system.

Speaking to the media, Bora linked the issues of reforms in the education system and students’ rights with the UAPA accused Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam. Blatantly whitewashing the charges against Khalid and Imam, Neha Bora claimed that ‘Godi Media’ and the ‘BJP IT Cell’ have declared them as traitors.

She referred to the anti-Hindu Delhi riots conspiracy accused as “ordinary students” and claimed that they were being subjected to “political prosecution”. She raised questions on the judiciary by pointing out that Khalid and Imam have been languishing in jail for years, as they were not granted bail. However, she cleverly conceals the fact that the Supreme Court had denied bail to Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam, observing that a prima facie case was made out against them in connection with the 2020 anti-Hindu Delhi riots conspiracy.

Neha Bora’s so-called students’ rights activism is not limited to whitewashing serious crimes like inciting riots or communal tensions; she openly advocates and promotes hatred against the Brahmin community in the name of countering caste inequality. In a post pinned on her X profile, Bora uses ‘Brahmanvaad’ (Brahmanism) as an umbrella term to refer to all kinds of discrimination prevalent in society. She defines Brahmanism as “the historical suppression of one section by another section of society”. By her logic, any discrimination in Indian society, even if it has nothing to do with caste, could be attributed to Brahmanism.

body:
**Facts on Sonam Wangchuk hunger strike at Jantar Mantar:**

- Wangchuk began an **indefinite hunger strike** today (28 June 2026) at Jantar Mantar, joining the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) protest over exam irregularities (e.g. NEET) and demanding accountability from Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

- CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke alleges Delhi Police cut water/sanitation after the strike started, public toilets have no water, and a portable toilet was denied despite health concerns for Wangchuk.

- **Delhi Police denial** (DCP New Delhi official tweet): The allegations are “falsehoods and misinformation.” Police have **no role** in providing or maintaining water or sanitation facilities at the site.

Public toilets and civic amenities at Jantar Mantar fall under municipal bodies (MCD), not Delhi Police. The CJP protest has run since 20 June with occasional prior facility complaints.

No independent confirmation of deliberate police cutoff today. This is allegation vs official denial.

body:
**Fact check on the claims:**

- **NEET exam date**: Correct. The NEET (UG) 2026 re-exam (after May cancellation over leaks) was held June 21, 2026.

- **Students moved on**: Plausible. Results pending; many preparing next steps or other exams.

- **CJP protest & NEET connection**: Misleading. The Cockroach Janata Party (CJP), led by Abhijeet Dipke, is explicitly protesting alleged NEET paper leaks/exam irregularities at Jantar Mantar. Youth and students are participating. Sonam Wangchuk joined with an indefinite hunger strike from June 28 supporting these demands (plus Ladakh issues).

- **"No one connected to NEET" & "using as shield"**: False on connection; opinion on motives. The protest centers on exam accountability and calls for Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation.

- **"Without permission" & "instigating"**: Subjective. Jantar Mantar protests are routine; the sit-in/hunger strike is public and ongoing.

- **Call for "strictest action"**: Opinion. Authorities monitor such protests; no widespread reports of illegality here.

The post mixes verified timing with partisan dismissal of a real youth-led exam protest. CJP is satirical in name but focused on education grievances.

Article:- Sonam Wangchuk’s Hunger Strike Enters 17th Day Amid:- 
Growing Health Concerns
Educator and climate activist Sonam Wangchuk has reached the 17th day of an indefinite hunger strike at Delhi's Jantar Mantar, sparking urgent appeals from political leaders and public figures for him to end his fast as his health rapidly deteriorates.
The Cause and Demands
Wangchuk joined an ongoing protest led by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on June 28, 2026. The primary focus of the agitation is the demand for the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over alleged widespread irregularities in NEET and other national examinations.
Additionally, the protesters are seeking ₹1 crore in compensation for the families of students who allegedly died by suicide due to the fallout and stress of these examination irregularities.
Deteriorating Health
The prolonged fast is taking a severe toll on the 59-year-old activist. According to health updates shared by the CJP, Wangchuk has lost approximately 8.5 kilograms since beginning his strike. His blood glucose levels recently dropped to a concerning 67 mg/dL, and his blood pressure was recorded at 107/70 mm Hg. CJP spokespersons have stated that he is losing muscle mass and is in immense pain, warning that the coming days will be critical.
Growing Political and Public Support
As the medical crisis deepens, a growing chorus of prominent voices has expressed solidarity with the movement while urging Wangchuk to break his fast.
 *Political Leaders: Figures such as Akhilesh Yadav, Arvind Kejriwal, Uddhav Thackeray, and Mahua Moitra have voiced their support. Yadav and Kejriwal have publicly appealed to Wangchuk to end the fast, emphasizing that his life is too valuable to risk.
 *Civil Society: A group of eminent citizens, including writer Arundhati Roy and actors Naseeruddin Shah and Ratna Pathak Shah, have also backed the demand for the Education Minister's resignation while urging the protesters to prioritize their health.
Despite the mounting pleas, Wangchuk has refused to end his strike, reportedly telling supporters to ask the government why they refuse to open a dialogue instead of asking him to eat. The protesters are now planning a peaceful march to Parliament on July 20, strategically timed to coincide with the opening day of the Monsoon Session, to further escalate their demands.

body:
Actor Omi Vaidya, best known for playing Chatur in the film 3 Idiots, has expressed support for educator and climate activist Sonam Wangchuk, who entered the 17th day of his indefinite hunger strike.

In a video shared on social media, Vaidya referred to Aamir Khan's character Phunsukh Wangdu, widely regarded as being inspired by Wangchuk, and appealed to the public to pay attention to the activist's deteriorating health and the issues behind his protest.

"I don't want Phunsukh Wangdu to die," Vaidya said, urging people to learn more about Wangchuk's work and the reasons for his hunger strike. He also recalled meeting Wangchuk and described him as a remarkable individual.

According to the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which is leading the protest at Jantar Mantar, Wangchuk has lost nearly 9 kilograms since beginning his fast, and his health has continued to decline.

The CJP's protest, which began over alleged irregularities in the NEET examination, has expanded to include demands for the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, compensation for the families of NEET aspirants who allegedly died by suicide, and broader reforms in the examination system. The organisation has also announced a peaceful march to Parliament on July 20, the opening day of the Monsoon Session.

body:
The lukewarm response that the Cockroach Janta Party founders are witnessing at Jantar Mantar are the signs of the times we live in. Maasive following on Insta and Fb does not translate into on ground support. The generation which follows you on social media, especially the one's born post 2000, will not be willing to hit the streets. Heck, they are not even willing to walk down the road to get their daily household needs, because Blinkit, Zomato, Swiggy and their fourth friend Amazon, are all there, at their service. 

If only Urban Company and Pronto had an option, where one could hire protestors on one's behalf to protest for a cause, then the dwindling prospects of Cockroach Janta Party would have got a massive boost, but as of now, that functionality is not provided, but you never know.

Second, the faces of this movement lack charisma and public connect. Abhijeet Dipke is no mass leader, like Arvind Kejriwal, his persona and his background does not make the person behind the screen go like 'Woah, he is the guy I am willing to take 1 day off from my office'. 

Saurav Das and the other fellow, who keeps dancing to songs of 1990's Bollywood are not even Twitter celebrities. Also why would the generation following them, born post 2000, vibe to songs of Bollywood movies of 90's and the era of 2000 to 2010.

I did enjoy their dance performance, but then I am not your target audience. Similarly for all of Sonam Wangchuk's achievements, he too is no Anna Hazare and India of 2026, is not India of 2012. Life in India has become more comfortable, while the income disparity remains, both these truths run parallel. 

The issue of NEET, Ethanol are the one's which the ruling government should be rightly questioned about and one can even see supporters of the current government taking them to task on these 2 major issues.

However, the fast unto death emotional blackmail type of protest is passe. It no longer appeals to the current generation, neither to the one's previous to them, who actually grew up watching such protests overturn governments of the day.

A few days back, came across a clip of my friend @Iyervval where he spoke about how we don't realize that how far India has come from the days of abject poverty and this is where the answer to the lack of response to CJP's Dharna Party lies.

More than anything else, it is the lack of imagination on behalf of CJP, and taking a traditional route, which finds itself a lost child in today's comfort at the drop of an app button playstore.

Meanwhile, it is activist and News influencer @tehseenp 's campaign highlighting the issue of Ethanol that is drawing more attention, where in the elected representatives of the day,are being grudingly forced to acknowledge the issue.

May be, just may be, CJP folks study what AIM and Tehseen are saying and take a leaf out of their book.

2026 is not 2012!

body:
The #BJP led Union Government has repeatedly come under criticism over the handling of national-level entrance examinations, including #NEET. Despite multiple controversies, Union Education Minister #DharmendraPradhan continues to remain in office. What message does this send to the millions of students and parents across India who expect accountability from the government?

This year's NEET examination has been marred by numerous irregularities. Allegations have ranged from question paper leaks to students being allotted examination centres in foreign countries, while others, including candidates from Jammu & Kashmir, were assigned centres in distant states such as Rajasthan. These incidents have raised serious concerns about the transparency and fairness of the examination process. Yet, there appears to be little visible urgency or accountability from the Union Education Minister.

The responsibility for addressing these concerns ultimately rests with the Union Government. If such large scale irregularities have occurred, the Education Minister should take responsibility. Instead, there is a growing perception that the government has failed to adequately address the anxieties of students and parents.

Prime Minister #NarendraModi, who has the authority to act against his ministers, is perceived by critics as prioritising official foreign visits while dissatisfaction continues to grow at home. They argue that India's global image carries greater meaning when the concerns of its own citizens are addressed first.

Meanwhile, members of the Cockroach Janta Party (@CJP_2029) and education activist Sonam Wangchuk have been on a hunger strike for over two weeks, demanding accountability and reforms. Supporters of the protest believe the government's response has been inadequate despite the prolonged demonstration.

A government's greatest achievement is not merely governing the country, but governing in accordance with the aspirations and concerns of its people. When public sentiment and governmental priorities appear to diverge, celebrating achievements alone is unlikely to inspire confidence. Leadership earns respect through accountability, responsiveness, and a willingness to correct mistakes.

In Tamilnadu, the NEET examination has been associated with several student suicides over the years, making the issue especially sensitive. There is an urgent need either to abolish NEET altogether or to comprehensively reform the examination system so that it is conducted fairly, transparently, and without placing excessive psychological pressure on students. Every deserving student should be able to write the examination in a just, stress free, and equitable environment.

Above all, Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan should accept responsibility for the latest irregularities and resign from his post. The demands raised through the CJP led protest deserve serious consideration, and those supporting the movement hope it succeeds in bringing meaningful accountability and reforms to India's education system. @abhijeet_dipke @CJP_for_India #PradhanGoBack

body:
The #BJP led Union Government has repeatedly come under criticism over the handling of national-level entrance examinations, including #NEET. Despite multiple controversies, Union Education Minister #DharmendraPradhan continues to remain in office. What message does this send to the millions of students and parents across India who expect accountability from the government?

This year's NEET examination has been marred by numerous irregularities. Allegations have ranged from question paper leaks to students being allotted examination centres in foreign countries, while others, including candidates from Jammu & Kashmir, were assigned centres in distant states such as Rajasthan. These incidents have raised serious concerns about the transparency and fairness of the examination process. Yet, there appears to be little visible urgency or accountability from the Union Education Minister.

The responsibility for addressing these concerns ultimately rests with the Union Government. If such large scale irregularities have occurred, the Education Minister should take responsibility. Instead, there is a growing perception that the government has failed to adequately address the anxieties of students and parents.

Prime Minister #NarendraModi, who has the authority to act against his ministers, is perceived by critics as prioritising official foreign visits while dissatisfaction continues to grow at home. They argue that India's global image carries greater meaning when the concerns of its own citizens are addressed first.

Meanwhile, members of the Cockroach Janta Party (@CJP_2029) and education activist Sonam Wangchuk have been on a hunger strike for over two weeks, demanding accountability and reforms. Supporters of the protest believe the government's response has been inadequate despite the prolonged demonstration.

A government's greatest achievement is not merely governing the country, but governing in accordance with the aspirations and concerns of its people. When public sentiment and governmental priorities appear to diverge, celebrating achievements alone is unlikely to inspire confidence. Leadership earns respect through accountability, responsiveness, and a willingness to correct mistakes.

In Tamilnadu, the NEET examination has been associated with several student suicides over the years, making the issue especially sensitive. There is an urgent need either to abolish NEET altogether or to comprehensively reform the examination system so that it is conducted fairly, transparently, and without placing excessive psychological pressure on students. Every deserving student should be able to write the examination in a just, stress free, and equitable environment.

Above all, Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan should accept responsibility for the latest irregularities and resign from his post. The demands raised through the CJP led protest deserve serious consideration, and those supporting the movement hope it succeeds in bringing meaningful accountability and reforms to India's education system. @abhijeet_dipke @CJP_for_India #PradhanGoBack

body:
Some people who joined CJP protest:

1) Arundhati Roy, who believes that Kashmir is not a part of India.

2) Colin Gonsalves, who filed a mercy petition for 26/11 terrorist Ajmal Kasab.

3) Prashant Bhushan, who approached Supreme Court at midnight to stop the hanging of terrorist Yakub Memon.

4) Nandita Narain, who sang "Bas naam rahega Allah ka" from CJP stage, a poem by Pakistani poet Faiz Ahmad Faiz.

5) Kunal Kamra, who said from CJP stage - "Yeh log Sita ke Pati ka naam lekar, Nita ke Pati ka kaam kar rahe hain" (They chant the name of Sita's husband, but they serve Nita's husband).

At what point does this even look like a protest against the NEET paper leak? If the objective was truly to seek justice for NEET students, the stage should have been given to the students who were affected by the paper leak, or to the parents whose children lost their lives due to the paper leak. Instead, the platform was given to the Islamo-left ecosystem. It clearly shows the CJP protest organizers' priorities and the real agenda behind the protest.

Sonam Wangchuk should also take a closer look at what is happening around him. He has been reduced to a pawn while others are using his credibility and public image to lend legitimacy to the movement.

A few days ago, Sonam Wangchuk himself remarked from the CJP stage that others were eating at the protest while he was on a hunger strike. He openly expressed disappointment and said - "If you cannot join me in an indefinite hunger strike, at least observe a one-day hunger strike, or skip one meal in solidarity." How many CJP protest organizers acted on his appeal?

He should analyze whether his struggle is being used to advance a broader political or ideological agenda rather than the cause that people believe he is representing, because the CJP protest appears to have become a platform for everything except the NEET paper leak.

By @AskAnshul

body:
The Hijacking of Student Anger: Exposing Abhijeet Dipke, CJP, and the Political Drift of the NEET Protests

The NEET paper leak crisis of 2026 triggered one of the biggest student movements in recent years. Lakhs of aspirants saw their futures thrown into uncertainty, while several families suffered unimaginable loss. The protests initially focused on a single demand—accountability for the examination system and action against those responsible for the leak. However, critics argue that what began as a student-led movement gradually transformed into a broader political platform under the leadership of Abhijeet Dipke and the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP).

Dipke, a former Aam Aadmi Party social media operative, launched CJP in May 2026. The organisation rapidly gained millions of followers online and positioned itself as the voice of frustrated students. Its stated demands included the resignation of the Education Minister, compensation for affected families, and structural reforms to prevent future paper leaks. Yet as protests expanded across cities, observers noted that the movement increasingly attracted political organisations and ideological groups whose agendas extended well beyond education.

Left-leaning student organisations such as the Students' Federation of India (SFI), the All India Students' Association (AISA), and Krantikari Yuva Sangathan (KYS) became prominent participants. Opposition leaders and public figures also visited protest sites, while activist Sonam Wangchuk's hunger strike added national attention. Critics argued that these developments shifted the focus from examination reforms to wider political narratives.

The controversy intensified after actor Prakash Raj publicly stated at a protest that he would not chant Jai Shri Ram. His remarks, along with comments about not caring if protesters were labelled terrorists or Pakistanis, became one of the most debated moments of the movement. Separately, a performance of Faiz Ahmed Faiz's poetry at the protest drew complaints from Hindu organisations, which alleged that it hurt religious sentiments. These incidents fuelled accusations that the protests were no longer centred solely on student welfare.

Dipke himself attracted criticism after stating during an interview that if he were Muslim like Umar Khalid, he would already be in jail. Around the same period, photographs showing CJP spokesperson Saurav Das with Umar Khalid circulated online, leading critics to question the ideological associations surrounding the movement. Although supporters dismissed these concerns as political attacks, opponents argued that they reflected a broader shift away from educational issues.

Questions were also raised about funding and organisational transparency. CJP maintained that its activities were driven by volunteers and public support. However, critics questioned how a movement that organised nationwide protests, legal campaigns, and extensive media outreach could sustain such operations without greater financial backing or institutional support.

Ultimately, the biggest criticism of CJP is not that it protested the NEET paper leak, but that it allegedly allowed the movement to become politically and ideologically polarised. Many believe students deserved a united campaign focused exclusively on examination reforms and accountability. Instead, the protests became associated with controversies involving religion, political symbolism, and ideological conflict.

Whether one views CJP as a genuine youth movement or a politically influenced campaign, the debate surrounding its role continues. The 2026 NEET protests remain a reminder of how quickly a movement built around legitimate student grievances can evolve into a much broader political confrontation.

body:
A friend wrote the other day that LinkedIn posts are like moral science stories. Mine here is sounding like that i think. Just watched SBS World News in Australia, covering environmentalist and engineer Sonam Wangchuk's hunger strike and his removal from Jantar Mantar by police over concerns for his health. Hence the outpouring. 

Like many in the diaspora, I follow the news from back home closely, but what troubles me these days is not just the news itself, but how difficult it has become to talk about India without being immediately pushed into one political camp or another. You know, question anything about the current Modi govt and be branded anti-national or a Pakistani.

Been following Jantar Mantar. To be honest, I'm not a fan of Abhijeet Dipke's voice. Sorry that is just my aesthetics at play, very shallow yes :), but whatever one's politics, the Cockroach Janata Party is focussing on something that is affecting the futures of millions of young people and deserve to be discussed seriously, not dismissed because they are politically inconvenient.

I know perfectly well how things function in India. I remember applying for my first passport in 1993. The police verification officer found everything in order, but still hinted that he expected chai-pani ka kharcha. Also, my father, a government servant, always told me that the person who gives a bribe is no better than the person who takes one. Ofc, I was going to stick to this, especially when I was a student and verging on broke. Thankfully, I still received my passport.

Corruption, bureaucratic hurdles and the struggle for opportunities are not new problems in India. Everyone knows that, come on! But then I scroll through my feed and see some friends calling these protesters "planted" to smear the government. Really? Are they not seeing what's right in front of us? The job crisis, the falling rupee, the shaky economic indicators – it's all there. Ugggghhhhhh.

How is it wrong to agree with facts that are clearly visible? I love India - no one can take that away from me but this whole "all is well, Modi is God" narrative? That, I genuinely don't get. 

Btw, do watch News Pinch @TheNewspinch. They have some of the most powerful interviews from this protest at Jantar Mantar.

#SonamWangchuk Hospitalised After 21-Day #HungerStrike; #CJP Founder #AbhishekDipke attacked with #Ink | Protest Sparks Political Row

Activist, engineer, and education reformer Sonam Wangchuk was shifted to #Safdarjung Hospital by #DelhiPolice on Saturday after his indefinite hunger strike at Jantar Mantar entered its 21st day and his health reportedly deteriorated.

According to Delhi Police, the action was taken on the advice of medical experts and in compliance with the directions of the Delhi High Court, which had ordered regular monitoring of Wangchuk's health. In an official statement, the Deputy Commissioner of Police, New Delhi, said Wangchuk was moved to the hospital for "essential medical care" and appealed to protesters to vacate the protest site peacefully.

Supporters of Wangchuk, however, alleged that plainclothes police personnel entered the protest stage, blocked public view using white sheets, and removed him against his will. They argued that the court had directed authorities to monitor his health rather than forcibly end the protest. These claims have not been independently verified.

The protest is linked to demands for accountability over the alleged #NEET examination #PaperLeak, with demonstrators seeking the resignation of Union #EducationMinister #DharmendraPradhan and broader reforms to the examination system.

Following Wangchuk's removal, #CockroachJanataParty founder #AbhijeetDipke announced an indefinite hunger strike at Jantar Mantar. During the protest, a woman allegedly threw blue ink at Dipke, briefly creating chaos at the site. Reacting to the incident, he said, "Blue is my colour. Jai Bhim."

Before being taken to the hospital, Wangchuk addressed supporters, saying, "I've grown weak from the outside, but I'm strong from within." His supporters claim he lost around 9.5 kilograms during the fast.

The incident has triggered sharp political reactions, with opposition leaders criticising the police action, while Delhi Police maintain that the decision was taken solely to ensure Wangchuk received urgent medical treatment in view of his deteriorating health.

body:
Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke's father on Saturday criticised the Centre over its handling of the ongoing student protests, questioning how the government could be so "merciless" towards students and asking whether it was waiting for someone to die.

Bhagwan Dipke's remarks came hours after his son launched an indefinite hunger strike at Jantar Mantar following the hospitalisation of activist Sonam Wangchuk, who was shifted to Safdarjung Hospital after his health deteriorated during a 20-day fast over alleged irregularities in the NEET examination.

Speaking to a Marathi news channel from Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar, Bhagwan Dipke expressed concern over his son's health while urging the government to engage with the protesting students.

"As a father, I am concerned about Abhijeet. I pray that God gives wisdom to Prime Minister Narendra Modi so that better sense prevails and the government listens to the agitating students. Students across the country are on hunger strike. Is the government waiting for someone to die?" he said.

He accused the government of ignoring the concerns of students and questioned its alleged indifference.

"Are these students from Pakistan or any other country? They are Indians. How can the government behave so mercilessly towards them?" he asked.

Bhagwan Dipke also warned that if the government continued to ignore the protesters' demands, he and other family members would travel to Delhi and join the indefinite hunger strike.

His wife also expressed concern over the situation, saying the government should have waited until after the planned July 20 Parliament march before shifting Wangchuk to the hospital.

"The protest in Delhi was peaceful. Abhijeet began his indefinite fast after Sonam Wangchuk was taken to hospital. We are worried about him. The government should have taken a decision after July 20," she said.

She added that only the government knew why the agitation was not being taken seriously.

The CJP protest is a platform for everything except the NEET paper leak. The stage was never given to the students who were affected by the paper leak, nor was it ever given to the parents whose children lost their lives because of the paper leak.

Sonam Wangchuk joined the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) protest at Jantar Mantar.

He began an indefinite hunger strike on June 28, 2026, demanding the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over alleged NEET-UG paper leaks and exam irregularities.

The Delhi High Court ordered daily medical monitoring and directed authorities to provide necessary medical intervention to protect his life.

On July 18 (Day 21 of the fast), Delhi Police shifted Wangchuk to Safdarjung Hospital, citing the court's order, expert medical advice, significant weight loss, and low blood sugar.

Delhi Police said protesters caused slight commotion during the transfer, but officers exercised maximum restraint.

CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke alleged Wangchuk was forcibly detained and accused police of assaulting protesters during the transfer.

Wangchuk's wife, Gitanjali J. Angmo, alleged she was not allowed to carry her mobile phone into his eighth-floor room, with access beyond the sixth floor heavily restricted by police.

Angmo also claimed medical reports were withheld and personal lawyers and doctors were not allowed to meet Wangchuk.

She publicly opposed any oral or intravenous treatment without the consent of the family and Wangchuk's monitoring doctors, questioned the need for hospitalization, said he had appeared fine the previous day, and noted no official police or hospital response to these specific allegations had been reported.
